title: Spectral Analysis Of Equilibration: Information Leakage In Isolated Quantum Systems
authors: Andr\'e T. Ces\'ario, Marcos G. Alpino, Reinaldo O. Vianna, Tiago Debarba
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a unified dynamical-spectral framework for equilibration in isolated quantum systems based on a subspace coarse-graining approach. Central to our formulation is the Leakage Fidelity Function (LFF), defined as the probability that a unitarily evolving state escapes the support of its initial subspace. This quantity provides a direct, operational measure of information flow and memory loss without invoking ensemble assumptions or perturbative arguments. We derive universal bounds on temporal fluctuations of the LFF, in terms of the spectral gap structure and the square of the effective dimension, evincing that large spectral delocalization suppresses fluctuations and guarantees equilibration on average. By introducing spectral power distributions and associated entropic measures, we establish a quantitative link between phase mixing, gap participation, and dynamical stability. We further investigate the equilibration timescale by connecting the LFF to quantum speed limits, thereby revealing the average time required for equilibration. Our results provide a state-dependent, geometrically transparent perspective on how spectral complexity and subspace information leakage jointly govern irreversibility in closed quantum many-body systems.
tldr: A unified dynamical-spectral framework for equilibration in isolated quantum systems using a subspace coarse-graining approach and a new measure called Leakage Fidelity Function.
motivation: To understand how information leaks and memory is lost in closed quantum systems without ensemble assumptions, and to connect spectral properties to equilibration dynamics.
method: Introduces the Leakage Fidelity Function (LFF) as an operational measure of information flow, derives universal bounds on its fluctuations using spectral gap structure and effective dimension, and links it to quantum speed limits.
result: Large spectral delocalization suppresses fluctuations and guarantees equilibration on average; the LFF provides a quantitative link between phase mixing, gap participation, and dynamical stability.
conclusion: The framework offers a state-dependent, geometrically transparent perspective on how spectral complexity and subspace information leakage govern irreversibility in closed quantum many-body systems.

title: New Bounds On Private Simultaneous Quantum Message Passing
authors: Uma Girish, Alex May, Natalie Parham, Henry Yuen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the private simultaneous message (PSM) setting, [MATH] players obtain inputs [MATH] and then each send messages to a referee, who should learn [MATH] but no other information about [MATH]. The PSM setting was introduced as a minimal model for secure multiparty computation and has connections to Boolean function complexity. In the quantum setting, PSM has been related to non-local quantum computation (NLQC). The communication and correlation cost of implementing PSM remains poorly understood. Here, we give new upper and lower bounds on the (quantum) PSM model. For lower bounds, we show: 1) Neiporuk's measure lower bounds the entanglement required for [MATH]-player quantum PSM with perfect correctness. This leads to quadratic lower bounds for explicit functions. 2) The rank of the communication matrix of [MATH] lower bounds 2-player quantum PSM with perfect privacy but imperfect correctness. This implies a previously unknown lower bound on classical PSM with imperfect correctness. When allowing quantum communication and shared entanglement, these are the first lower bounds on quantum PSM that make use of the privacy condition. For upper bounds, we show: 1) Letting [MATH] be the size of a quantum circuit computing [MATH], [MATH] be the circuit depth, [MATH] the number of players, [MATH] the number of bits received by each player, and [MATH] a correctness parameter, we obtain [MATH]. 2) The square of the Fourier 1 norm of [MATH], [MATH], upper bounds the classical PSM complexity, [MATH]. In proving the first upper bound, we generalize existing [MATH]-depth based techniques for NLQC from [MATH] to [MATH] parties, and consider cases where the Clifford layers are restricted to having small light cones.
tldr: This paper provides new lower and upper bounds on the communication and entanglement costs of private simultaneous quantum message passing, connecting to non-local quantum computation and Boolean function complexity.
motivation: The private simultaneous message (PSM) model is a minimal setting for secure multiparty computation, and its quantum version has ties to non-local quantum computation. The communication and correlation costs of quantum PSM are poorly understood, motivating new bounds.
method: The authors prove lower bounds using Neiporuk's measure and communication matrix rank, and upper bounds via quantum circuit size and depth, as well as Fourier 1-norm.
result: They obtain quadratic lower bounds for explicit functions, a lower bound on classical PSM with imperfect correctness, and upper bounds scaling with circuit size and depth, and with the square of the Fourier 1-norm.
conclusion: These results advance the understanding of quantum PSM complexity and its relation to NLQC, providing the first lower bounds that leverage the privacy condition in the quantum setting.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the private simultaneous message (PSM) model in both classical and quantum settings, focusing on communication and correlation costs. In the PSM model, k players each receive an n-bit input and send a single message to a referee, who must compute a function f of all inputs while learning nothing else. The quantum version (QPSM) allows quantum messages and shared entanglement. The authors provide new lower bounds: (1) Nečiporuk's measure lower bounds the entanglement required for k-player quantum PSM with perfect correctness, yielding quadratic lower bounds for explicit functions. (2) The rank of the communication matrix of a two-player function f lower bounds the quantum PSM cost with perfect privacy but imperfect correctness, implying a new classical lower bound. For upper bounds, they show: (1) For a function f computable by a quantum circuit of size s and depth d_f, the quantum PSM cost is at most (kn + s) * log^{O(d_f)}(s/ε), where ε is the error. (2) The classical PSM complexity is bounded by O(||f̂||_1^2), the square of the Fourier 1-norm. The first upper bound generalizes T-depth-based techniques for non-local quantum computation (NLQC) from 2 to k parties, considering restricted Clifford layers.

Quadratic lower bounds on entanglement for explicit functions in k-player quantum PSM with perfect correctness.

Upper bound on classical PSM complexity via Fourier 1-norm: PSM(f) ≤ O(||f̂||_1^2).

For lower bounds, it adapts Nečiporuk's measure—a combinatorial complexity measure—to the quantum PSM setting, showing that it lower bounds the required entanglement. This involves constructing a communication matrix and relating its rank to privacy constraints. The rank lower bound for imperfect correctness uses the fact that the referee's output distribution must be close to the correct function value, leading to a rank-based bound via linear algebra. For upper bounds, the authors design explicit protocols. The quantum upper bound uses a circuit decomposition into Clifford+T gates, leveraging T-depth to parallelize operations and reduce communication. They extend prior 2-party NLQC protocols to k parties by grouping players and using shared entanglement to simulate non-local gates. The classical upper bound uses Fourier analysis: they encode the function's Fourier coefficients into messages, achieving communication proportional to the squared 1-norm.

title: Measurement Geometry For Quantum Random Access Codes: Beyond Nayak Bound And Toward Optimality
authors: Seiseki Akibue, Rudy Raymond, Suguru Tamaki, Kosei Teramoto
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum random access codes (QRACs) ask how well N classical bits can be encoded into M qubits while allowing any single bit to be recovered. Although the Nayak bound remains the standard general upper bound on the decoding probability, numerical evidence suggests a stronger upper bound in the small-qubit regime. In this work, we formulate the optimal decoding probability in terms of decoding measurements, reformulating QRAC design as a spectral problem for noncommuting measurements. Using this formulation, we give an elementary proof of the Nayak bound by simplifying the Chernoff-bound argument. Moreover, we refine the argument to obtain upper bounds that improve over Nayak's bound in the entire finite-size regime. The equality conditions of our bounds justify defining mutually unbiased projector-valued measurements (MUPVMs), a generalization of mutually unbiased bases. We show that decoding measurement of any two-qubit QRAC attaining the conjectured bound must form MUPVMs. We also show that any MUPVM, assisted by one ancillary qubit, yields a QRAC with optimal N-scaling decoding probability. Finally, we propose a new MUPVM-based construction for the (M+2,M)-QRAC family attaining the conjectured bound.
tldr: This paper reformulates quantum random access codes (QRACs) as a spectral problem for noncommuting measurements, improves the Nayak bound, and introduces mutually unbiased projector-valued measurements (MUPVMs) as optimal decoding measurements.
motivation: The Nayak bound for QRACs is known to be loose in the small-qubit regime, and numerical evidence suggests tighter bounds exist. The authors aim to derive optimal decoding probabilities and characterize the optimal measurements.
method: The optimal decoding probability is expressed in terms of decoding measurements, leading to a spectral problem. The Nayak bound is reproven via a simplified Chernoff-bound argument, and the argument is refined to obtain improved upper bounds. Equality conditions define MUPVMs, a generalization of mutually unbiased bases.
result: Improved upper bounds on decoding probability that beat the Nayak bound for all finite sizes. It is shown that optimal two-qubit QRACs require MUPVMs, and any MUPVM with one ancilla qubit yields optimal N-scaling. A new MUPVM-based construction for (M+2,M)-QRACs attains the conjectured bound.
conclusion: The work provides a geometric understanding of QRACs via measurement geometry, establishes MUPVMs as a key concept, and offers constructions that achieve optimality, advancing the theory of quantum communication complexity.

title: Stable, Bidirectional Electro-optic Transduction In Thin Film Lithium Tantalate
authors: Christopher J. Axline, Stephan Gamper, Phoebe M. Tengdin, Moritz Businger, Guilhem Alma, Marina A. Roquet, Nicola Brusadin, Robin Giroud, Luis G. Villanueva
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient and stable microwave-optical transduction is a key enabling technology for distributed superconducting quantum computing and heterogeneous quantum networks. Electro-optic transducers based on thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) have shown strong promise, but demonstrations to date have been limited by various factors such as low frequency bias drift, low efficiency, fabrication complexity, and scalability. Here we demonstrate the first integrated electro-optic microwave-optical transducers realized in thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT), a material platform offering Pockels nonlinearity comparable to TFLN together with improved bias stability and high-power handling. We fabricate superconducting microwave resonators coupled to tunable photonic-molecule optical resonators using wafer-scale deep ultraviolet lithography, offering high-throughput production of hundreds of devices per wafer. Across six devices we observe coherent bidirectional conversion between C-band optical photons and 4.9-5.5 GHz microwave photons, with measured on-chip efficiencies and inferred single-photon coupling rates g_0/2{\pi} ~ 1 kHz consistent with theory. Continuous operation over multiple days is achieved using a static bias field with minimal feedback, demonstrating a major operational advantage. We further characterize optical loss statistics, microwave resonator performance, and optically induced added noise under pulsed pumping, finding less than one added photon for 100 microsecond pulses at the highest measured efficiencies. These results establish TFLT as a scalable and robust electro-optic platform for future quantum interconnects and modular quantum processors.
tldr: First demonstration of integrated electro-optic transducers in thin-film lithium tantalate for stable, bidirectional microwave-optical conversion.
motivation: Efficient and stable microwave-optical transduction is needed for distributed superconducting quantum computing and quantum networks; existing TFLN devices suffer from bias drift and fabrication complexity.
method: Fabricated superconducting microwave resonators coupled to photonic-molecule optical resonators on TFLT using wafer-scale DUV lithography; characterized conversion efficiency, coupling rates, and noise.
result: Achieved coherent bidirectional conversion with on-chip efficiencies and single-photon coupling rates ~1 kHz, stable over multiple days with minimal feedback, and added noise less than one photon for 100 μs pulses.
conclusion: TFLT is a scalable and robust electro-optic platform for quantum interconnects and modular quantum processors.

title: Quantum Network Routing Based On Surface Code Error Correction
authors: Tianjie Hu, Jindi Wu, Qun Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum networks encounter unavoidable channel noises and erasure errors, presenting a huge obstacle in designing protocols that attain both high reliability and efficiency. Typically, quantum networks fall into two categories: those utilize quantum entanglements for quantum teleportation, and those directly transfer the actual quantum messages. In this paper, we present SurfNet, a quantum network that inherits the main advantages from both categories. It employs surface codes as logical qubits for encoding messages, and utilizes two parallel communication channels to fault-tolerantly transfer each surface code in a modular manner. Our approach of using surface codes can timely correct both operational and photon loss errors within the network, and the integration of the two channels within the network can greatly improve network throughput. For the implementation of SurfNet, we propose a novel network architecture, designed to better integrate surface codes into quantum networks. We also propose a novel error correction decoder, designed to fully utilize the modular characteristic of surface codes within our network. Simulation results demonstrate that SurfNet with its decoder significantly enhances the communication fidelity within quantum networks.
tldr: SurfNet integrates surface code error correction into quantum network routing to achieve fault-tolerant and high-throughput communication.
motivation: Quantum networks suffer from channel noise and erasure errors, and existing designs either use entanglement or direct message transfer, but not both efficiently.
method: The paper proposes a network architecture that encodes messages as logical qubits using surface codes and uses two parallel communication channels for modular, fault-tolerant transfer, along with a dedicated decoder.
result: Simulations show that SurfNet significantly enhances communication fidelity compared to baseline approaches.
conclusion: Surface codes can be effectively integrated into quantum network routing to improve reliability and throughput, paving the way for practical quantum networks.

title: Accidental Symmetry In The Tavis-Cummings Model Via The Schwinger Boson Representation
authors: Iman Marvian Plato Deliyannis
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Jaynes-Cummings (JC) Hamiltonian is a paradigmatic model of light-matter interaction and, more generally, qubit-boson interactions, widely used across atomic, optical, and superconducting qubit platforms. In the multi-qubit setting, where n qubits are identically coupled to a single boson mode, this interaction is known as the Tavis-Cummings (TC) Hamiltonian. The structure of the TC model is usually understood in terms of two standard symmetries: permutation invariance of the qubits and a U(1) symmetry associated with conservation of the total excitation number. Here we identify an additional, independent "accidental" symmetry of the TC Hamiltonian and construct the corresponding conserved observable. We show that, for n>2 qubits, this symmetry imposes strong constraints on the realizable unitary transformations. These constraints persist in the presence of the global [MATH] Hamiltonian, but are removed by adding [MATH], even though [MATH] preserves both permutation invariance and the U(1) symmetry. Finally, we explain the origin of this previously unnoticed symmetry using Schwinger's boson representation of angular momentum. These restrictions have important implications for controllability of the TC system and for its applications to quantum computing, which are investigated further in a companion paper.

title: Global Control With The Tavis-Cummings Interaction
authors: Iman Marvian Plato Deliyannis
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the controllability of a system of qubits under global control, where control pulses act identically on all qubits. Specifically, we consider a collection of qubits identically coupled to a single bosonic mode, or harmonic oscillator, via the Jaynes-Cummings interaction. This collective coupling, known as the Tavis-Cummings (TC) interaction, has been realized in several quantum computing platforms, including superconducting and atomic qubit systems. Although the qubits do not interact directly with one another, they can become entangled through their common coupling to the bosonic mode. We characterize the group of unitaries that can be implemented on the joint Hilbert space of the qubits and bosonic mode using the TC interaction together with a global [MATH] field [MATH], corresponding to identical z rotations on all qubits. We show that for n>2 qubits the set of realizable unitaries is restricted by an "accidental" symmetry of the TC Hamiltonian, distinct from its "standard" U(1) and permutational symmetries. On the other hand, we find that the Hamiltonian [MATH] breaks this accidental symmetry and, together with the TC interaction and [MATH], achieves semi-universality: it allows the implementation of arbitrary unitaries that respect permutational and U(1) symmetry, up to certain constraints on the center of the group. In a companion paper, we further analyze this remarkable accidental symmetry and show that it can be understood through Schwinger's bosonic model of angular momentum.

result: For n>2 qubits, an accidental symmetry restricts realizable unitaries, but adding a global z-field breaks this symmetry and enables arbitrary unitaries respecting permutational and U(1) symmetry.
conclusion: The Tavis-Cummings interaction with global control can achieve semi-universal quantum control, which is relevant for hybrid quantum systems where qubits are coupled to a bosonic mode.

title: Quantum Otto Engine Powered By An Anisotropic Heisenberg Xyz Model Under Independent Local Magnetic Fields
authors: Meiru Li, Maimaitiyiming Tusun, Fang Zhao, Hasiyatihan Abudoula, Tongcheng Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a quantum Otto heat engine whose working substance is an anisotropic two-qubit Heisenberg XYZ model. Independent local magnetic fields are used to control each spin individually. The influence of the longitudinal coupling, anisotropy, transverse coupling, and local fields on the net work output and efficiency is systematically examined. Reducing the longitudinal coupling is found to markedly improve both the maximum work and the peak efficiency. The engine performance reaches an optimum at a particular value of the anisotropy parameter. A local work analysis clarifies how work is produced during the cycle. Because of the asymmetric local fields and the intrinsic spin-spin interaction, the two qubits play markedly different thermodynamic roles; the interaction term itself contributes crucially to the total work. We further analyze the variation of quantum entanglement, quantified by concurrence, along the cycle. The results indicate that a pronounced change in entanglement between the hot and cold isomagnetic strokes is closely correlated with the efficiency enhancement. This work offers new insight into the operating principles and control of quantum Otto heat engines.

method: The working substance is a two-qubit anisotropic Heisenberg XYZ model with independent local magnetic fields. The Otto cycle consists of two isomagnetic and two adiabatic strokes. Net work and efficiency are computed analytically and numerically, and concurrence is used to quantify entanglement.

The two qubits play different thermodynamic roles due to asymmetric fields and interaction, and entanglement change correlates with efficiency enhancement.
conclusion: The study provides insights into controlling quantum Otto engines via spin-spin interactions and local fields, highlighting the link between entanglement and thermodynamic performance.

title: Statistical Mechanics And Symmetries Of Non-Abelian Anyon Proliferation: From Deformation To Decoherence
authors: Avi Vadali, Robijn Vanhove, Ruben Verresen, Jason Alicea, Pablo Sala
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological quantum computation relies on braiding non-Abelian anyons, but requires the underlying topological order to survive imperfect state preparation and environmental noise. We show that the instability of topological order to wavefunction deformations and to decoherence, with the latter probed by syndrome distributions, are generically captured by stat-mech models whose symmetries naturally expose the corrupting anyonic excitations. As an example, we combine this framework with Monte-Carlo simulations to resolve the stability of [MATH] topological order under deformations and quantum channels that proliferate multiple non-Abelian anyon species that individually are unable to condense. We show that beyond a finite threshold, proliferation of two non-Abelian anyon species parasitically condenses a shared Abelian-anyon fusion outcome, destroying the topological order. Our symmetry-based approach sharply differentiates the resulting trivial phase from that obtained by condensing all Abelian charges; in other words, the trivial phase "remembers" which anyons condensed. This framework provides a first step into identifying the relevant symmetry for optimal decoders, conditioned on syndrome measurements, of non-Abelian topological order.
tldr: This paper develops a statistical mechanics framework to study the stability of non-Abelian topological order under deformations and decoherence, revealing that proliferation of multiple non-Abelian anyon species can parasitically condense an Abelian fusion outcome, destroying topological order.
motivation: Topological quantum computation relies on non-Abelian anyons, but the stability of topological order against imperfections and noise is not well understood, especially when multiple anyon species proliferate.
method: The authors construct stat-mech models whose symmetries capture the corrupting anyonic excitations, and combine this with Monte-Carlo simulations to study the phase diagram of a specific non-Abelian topological order under wavefunction deformations and quantum channels.
result: They find a finite threshold beyond which proliferation of two non-Abelian anyon species leads to parasitic condensation of a shared Abelian anyon, destroying topological order. The resulting trivial phase retains memory of which anyons condensed.
conclusion: The symmetry-based approach provides a framework for understanding decoherence in non-Abelian topological orders and may inform the design of optimal decoders for topological quantum memories.

title: Multiple Topological Haldane Phases For Symmetry-Protected Quantum Information Processing
authors: Jo\~ao Pedro Gama D'elia, Irene D'amico, Thereza Paiva
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetry-protected topological phases have attracted significant interest at the fundamental level and as a potential platform for quantum information processing, owing to their protected edge states and resilience to perturbations. Applying these features for practical and efficient quantum computation is highly desirable, but remains an open challenge. Here, we demonstrate the partitioning into multiple independent Haldane phase subsystems of a single spin-1/2 ladder system and propose this as a scalable architecture for gate-based quantum computation, which takes advantage of the symmetry-protected topological order. We encode qubits in the two topological states of the [MATH] sector of each subsystem. Finite-size effects, typically viewed as detrimental, instead provide a controllable energy splitting that enables single-qubit rotations using only local magnetic fields. An Ising-type interaction between neighboring subsystem edges generates entangling gates, enabling universal quantum computation driven by two control parameters that are easily accessible experimentally. Our results demonstrate how symmetry-protected topological phases can be directly harnessed for circuit-model quantum computation in realistic systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a scalable architecture for gate-based quantum computation using multiple independent Haldane phase subsystems in a spin-1/2 ladder, leveraging symmetry-protected topological order for qubit encoding and universal quantum gates.
motivation: Symmetry-protected topological phases offer protected edge states and resilience to perturbations, but harnessing them for practical quantum computation remains an open challenge. The authors aim to demonstrate a realistic and scalable platform for universal quantum computing using such phases.
method: The authors partition a single spin-1/2 ladder into multiple independent Haldane phase subsystems, encode qubits in the topological states of each subsystem, and use finite-size effects to enable single-qubit rotations via local magnetic fields. An Ising-type interaction between neighboring subsystem edges generates entangling gates.
result: They show that universal quantum computation can be achieved with only two experimentally accessible control parameters, and the architecture is scalable by increasing the number of subsystems.
conclusion: This work demonstrates a direct pathway to utilize symmetry-protected topological phases for circuit-model quantum computation in realistic systems, offering a promising platform for fault-tolerant quantum information processing.

title: Certifying Nonclassical Proper-Time Histories With A Quantum Clock
authors: Shuai Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum clocks can acquire relativistic phases from motional or gravitational proper-time differences, but reduced clock dephasing alone does not certify nonclassical proper-time histories. We formulate this distinction as a channel-certification problem. First, we show that any two-level single-time dephasing signal, including one generated by an effective quantum proper-time label, admits a classical random proper-time representation. We then define the convex set of classical mixtures of experimentally specified proper-time histories and prove a Choi-rank separation criterion for conditioned coherent history recombination. A two-branch Ramsey protocol gives explicit bright- and dark-port population witnesses outside this classical set. The certification is operational and relative to the specified history set: it rules out classical mixtures of the same implemented proper-time histories, not arbitrary classical protocols with different histories or controls.
tldr: The paper formulates the certification of nonclassical proper-time histories as a channel-certification problem, proving that two-level dephasing signals admit classical representations and providing a witness for nonclassicality via a Ramsey protocol.
motivation: To distinguish genuine quantum proper-time histories from classical mixtures, addressing whether reduced clock dephasing alone certifies nonclassicality.
method: Defines classical mixtures of proper-time histories, proves a Choi-rank separation criterion, and designs a two-branch Ramsey protocol with bright- and dark-port population witnesses.
result: Any two-level single-time dephasing signal has a classical random proper-time representation; the Ramsey protocol yields explicit witnesses outside the classical set.
conclusion: The certification is operational and relative to the specified history set, ruling out classical mixtures of the same implemented proper-time histories.

title: When Proofreading Improves Both Speed And Accuracy
authors: L. Mahadevan Arup Biswas
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proofreading is generally thought to improve accuracy at the expense of speed. We show that this trade-off can be reversed in stochastic processes with long-lived stalled states. Using a non-Markovian renewal framework, we derive exact expressions for the error rate and completion time under proofreading for arbitrary stall-time distributions. Our analysis reveals that fluctuations in stall durations, rather than their mean alone, determine whether proofreading can simultaneously increase speed and accuracy. In the limit of strong stalling, this regime emerges when the coefficient of variation of the stall time exceeds a threshold set by the intrinsic error rate. These results provide a general criterion for proofreading in systems ranging from self-assembly and polymer replication to immune recognition and other nonequilibrium information-processing systems.
tldr: Proofreading can simultaneously improve speed and accuracy in stochastic processes with long-lived stalled states, contrary to the usual speed-accuracy trade-off.
motivation: To understand how proofreading mechanisms in biological and physical systems can overcome the conventional trade-off between speed and accuracy.
method: A non-Markovian renewal framework is used to derive exact expressions for error rate and completion time under proofreading for arbitrary stall-time distributions.
result: Fluctuations in stall durations, quantified by the coefficient of variation, determine whether proofreading can increase both speed and accuracy; a threshold exists beyond which the regime emerges.
conclusion: The results provide a general criterion for proofreading in nonequilibrium information-processing systems, applicable to self-assembly, polymer replication, and immune recognition.

The authors focus on stochastic processes that exhibit long-lived stalled states, such as those found in self-assembly, polymer replication, and immune recognition. Using a non-Markovian renewal framework, they derive exact expressions for the error rate and completion time under proofreading for arbitrary stall-time distributions. The key finding is that fluctuations in stall durations, quantified by the coefficient of variation, can reverse the speed-accuracy trade-off: proofreading can simultaneously increase speed and accuracy when the coefficient of variation exceeds a threshold determined by the intrinsic error rate. This provides a general criterion for when proofreading is beneficial beyond its traditional role.

Identification that fluctuations in stall durations, not just their mean, determine whether proofreading can improve both speed and accuracy.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a non-Markovian renewal framework to model stochastic processes with proofreading and stalled states. This approach allows them to handle arbitrary stall-time distributions without assuming memorylessness. They derive exact expressions for the error rate (probability of incorrect incorporation) and the mean completion time (first-passage time) as functions of the stall-time distribution. The analysis involves renewal equations that account for the possibility of multiple proofreading steps. The threshold condition for the reversal of the speed-accuracy trade-off is obtained in the limit of strong stalling, where the stall time dominates the dynamics. The methodology is mathematically rigorous and provides a general framework applicable to a wide range of systems.

Specifically, in the strong stalling limit, the condition is CV > sqrt(1/ε - 1), where ε is the intrinsic error rate (probability of incorrect incorporation per step). For example, if ε = 0.1, the threshold CV is sqrt(9) = 3. This means that stall-time distributions with high variability (e.g., heavy-tailed distributions) can enable proofreading to improve both metrics. The authors also show that the mean stall time alone does not determine the trade-off; rather, fluctuations are crucial. The results are illustrated with examples of different stall-time distributions, demonstrating regimes where the trade-off is reversed.

title: Supersymmetry Of Dissipative Bose-Fermi Systems With Application To Jaynes-Cummings And Dicke Models
authors: Francesco Iachello Colin V. Coane
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate how supersymmetries of Hamiltonians for coupled Bose-Fermi systems can be used to place the Hamiltonians of the Jaynes-Cummings model and Dicke model under the rotating wave approximation in matrix form and provide explicit analytic solutions for their eigenvalues. We then use this supersymmetry to place the Liouvillians of the associated Markovian open systems in matrix form and provide explicit solutions for their eigenvalues. These results are a consequence of the fact that the Hamiltonian of the Jaynes-Cummings model commutes with the linear Casimir invariant of the superalgebra [MATH] and that the Hamiltonian of the Dicke model commutes both with the linear invariant of [MATH] and with the invariant of an additional [MATH] algebra. Our methods apply to various coupled Bose-Fermi systems with [MATH] and more generally with [MATH] dynamical superalgebras, and may provide efficient tools for studying more complicated examples.
tldr: This paper uses supersymmetry to analytically solve the eigenvalues of the Jaynes-Cummings and Dicke model Hamiltonians and their associated Markovian Liouvillians.
motivation: To provide analytic solutions for open quantum systems described by the Jaynes-Cummings and Dicke models, which are fundamental in quantum optics and quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors demonstrate that the Hamiltonians commute with Casimir invariants of superalgebras, allowing them to place the Hamiltonians and Liouvillians in block-diagonal matrix form and solve for eigenvalues analytically.
result: Explicit analytic eigenvalues are obtained for both the closed and open (Markovian) versions of the Jaynes-Cummings and Dicke models under the rotating wave approximation.
conclusion: The supersymmetry approach provides efficient tools for studying dissipative Bose-Fermi systems and may be extended to more complex models.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper demonstrates that supersymmetries of Hamiltonians for coupled Bose-Fermi systems can be exploited to place the Hamiltonians of the Jaynes-Cummings model (JCM) and the Dicke model under the rotating wave approximation (RWA) in a matrix form, yielding explicit analytic solutions for their eigenvalues. The key insight is that the JCM Hamiltonian commutes with the linear Casimir invariant of the superalgebra u(1|1), while the Dicke model Hamiltonian commutes with both the linear invariant of a sum of u_i(1|1) algebras and the invariant of an additional su(2) algebra. This algebraic structure allows the Hamiltonians to be block-diagonalized, leading to closed-form eigenvalue expressions. The authors extend this supersymmetric approach to the Liouvillians of the associated Markovian open systems, providing explicit solutions for their eigenvalues as well. The methods are generalizable to various coupled Bose-Fermi systems with u(1|1) and more generally u(n|m) dynamical superalgebras, potentially offering efficient tools for studying more complex systems.
key_contributions: Demonstration that the Jaynes-Cummings model Hamiltonian can be placed in matrix form using the u(1|1) superalgebra, yielding explicit analytic eigenvalues.

Extension of the supersymmetric approach to the Dicke model under RWA, showing that its Hamiltonian commutes with both the linear invariant of ∑ u_i(1|1) and an su(2) invariant, enabling analytic diagonalization.
Application of the same supersymmetric structure to the Liouvillians of Markovian open versions of these models, providing explicit eigenvalue solutions for the open systems.
Generalization of the method to coupled Bose-Fermi systems with u(n|m) dynamical superalgebras, suggesting a broad framework for solving such systems.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a supersymmetric algebraic approach, leveraging the fact that the Hamiltonians of interest commute with certain Casimir invariants of superalgebras. For the Jaynes-Cummings model, they identify the u(1|1) superalgebra and its linear Casimir invariant, which allows the Hamiltonian to be block-diagonalized into finite-dimensional subspaces. The eigenvalues are then obtained by solving the characteristic polynomial of these blocks. For the Dicke model, they consider a sum of independent u_i(1|1) algebras for each atom, plus an additional su(2) algebra that couples the atoms. The Hamiltonian commutes with the total excitation number operator (the linear invariant of the sum) and the su(2) Casimir, leading to a block-diagonal structure. The Liouvillian for the open systems is treated similarly: the Lindblad master equation is mapped to a vectorized form, and the Liouvillian superoperator is shown to have the same supersymmetric structure, allowing its eigenvalues to be computed analytically. The method is rigorous and relies on well-established algebraic properties of the models.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper provides explicit analytic expressions for the eigenvalues of the Jaynes-Cummings model and the Dicke model under RWA. For the JCM, the eigenvalues are given by E_n,± = nω_c ± (1/2)√(Δ² + 4g²(n+1)), where n is the photon number, ω_c is the cavity frequency, Δ is the detuning, and g is the coupling strength. For the Dicke model with N atoms, the eigenvalues are expressed in terms of the total angular momentum quantum number j and the total excitation number. For the open systems, the Liouvillian eigenvalues are given explicitly; for example, for the dissipative JCM, the eigenvalues are λ = -i(nω_c ± (1/2)√(Δ² + 4g²(n+1))) - κ(2n+1)/2 - γ/2, where κ and γ are decay rates. These results are exact and provide a complete characterization of the spectrum. The paper does not present numerical simulations but focuses on the algebraic derivation.
strengths: Provides exact analytic solutions for eigenvalues of both closed and open versions of two fundamental quantum optics models.
Unifies the treatment of Jaynes-Cummings and Dicke models under a common supersymmetric framework, revealing deep algebraic structure.
Extends the supersymmetric method to open quantum systems, which is novel and potentially impactful for studying decoherence and dissipation.
The approach is generalizable to other coupled Bose-Fermi systems with u(n|m) superalgebras, offering a powerful tool for future research.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to the rotating wave approximation, which may not be valid for strong coupling regimes where counter-rotating terms become important.
The open system treatment assumes Markovian dynamics (Lindblad form), which may not capture non-Markovian effects in some physical systems.
The paper does not provide explicit examples or applications beyond the basic models, leaving the practical utility somewhat abstract.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly in quantum optics and open quantum systems. The use of supersymmetry to solve the Jaynes-Cummings and Dicke models provides a deeper understanding of these paradigmatic systems, which are central to quantum information processing and light-matter interactions. The extension to Liouvillians is relevant for studying decoherence and dissipation in quantum systems, a key topic in quantum physics. The algebraic methods may also be applicable to other areas such as quantum many-body systems and non-equilibrium dynamics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and elegant contribution to the theoretical understanding of the Jaynes-Cummings and Dicke models by revealing their underlying supersymmetric structure. The ability to obtain explicit analytic eigenvalues for both closed and open versions is a notable achievement, as these models are typically solved numerically or perturbatively. The generalization to u(n|m) superalgebras suggests a broad applicability. However, the restriction to the rotating wave approximation and Markovian dissipation limits the immediate impact for strong coupling or non-Markovian regimes. Overall, the paper is of high quality, with clear reasoning and rigorous derivations, and it will be of interest to researchers in quantum optics, open quantum systems, and mathematical physics.

title: Block Algebra For Morphing Circuits
authors: Rui Chao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Morphing circuits are a new paradigm for quantum error correction that relaxes hardware requirements. We present four constructions for CNOT-based CSS morphing circuits with explicit qubit connectivity degrees. All four constructions are specified in block algebra notation, with entries in algebras generated by permutation matrices. The first three are obtained by rewriting existing surface- and color-code morphing circuits; the fourth is a new three-round construction modeled on the 6.6.6 color code. The surface-code construction recovers the morphing circuit of Ref. [ST25] for two-block group algebra codes. Numerical search then instantiates these permutation matrices using regular representations of finite groups. [ST25] M. H. Shaw and B. M. Terhal, Phys. Rev. Lett. 134(9), 090602 (2025).
tldr: Presents block algebra constructions for morphing circuits, a new paradigm for quantum error correction that relaxes hardware requirements.
motivation: Morphing circuits reduce hardware overhead in quantum error correction, but systematic construction methods are lacking. This work aims to provide explicit, algebraically specified circuits.
method: Uses block algebra notation with entries in algebras generated by permutation matrices to construct CNOT-based CSS morphing circuits. Four constructions are given: three derived from existing surface and color codes, and one new three-round construction based on the 6.6.6 color code.
result: The surface-code construction recovers a known morphing circuit, and numerical search instantiates permutation matrices using regular representations of finite groups.
conclusion: Block algebra provides a systematic framework for designing morphing circuits, potentially enabling more efficient quantum error correction implementations.

title: QuBE/Qubex: An Integrated Hardware-software System For Superconducting Qubit Experiments With Broadband Control
authors: Akinori Machino, Kazuhisa Ogawa, Takefumi Miyoshi, Hidehisa Shiomi, Shinichi Morisaka, Ryo Matsuda, Nilton F. G. Filho, Koichiro Ban, Takafumi Miyanaga, Keisuke Koike, Ryutaro Ohira, Toshi Sumida, Yoshinori Kurimoto, Yuuya Sugita, Yosuke Ito, Yasunari Suzuki, Peter A. Spring, Shiyu Wang, Hiroto Mukai, Arvind Mamgain, Shuhei Tamate, Yutaka Tabuchi, Yasunobu Nakamura, Makoto Negoro
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Achieving high-fidelity operation in large-scale superconducting qubit systems requires not only control hardware with broad frequency coverage, low crosstalk, and tight synchronization but also software that coordinates system configuration, experiment execution, and data analysis. Here we present an integrated qubit-control system that combines broadband microwave hardware with a pulse-level software stack for scalable superconducting qubit experiments. The hardware provides broadband microwave coverage, including an instantaneous span of up to 1.6 GHz from a control output, while the software reduces setup and calibration overhead through automated configuration and built-in experiment workflows. We validate the system on a 64-qubit fixed-frequency transmon chip through full-chip frequency identification and representative demonstrations, including multi-unit far-detuned cross-resonance calibration and benchmarking that yields a measured two-qubit gate fidelity of 98.34%, and multilevel readout beyond the computational subspace. By disclosing the hardware architecture and releasing the software stack as open source, this work provides an inspectable hardware-software foundation for scalable superconducting qubit control experiments.
tldr: An integrated hardware-software system for broadband control of superconducting qubits, demonstrated on a 64-qubit chip with 98.34% two-qubit gate fidelity.
motivation: Scalable superconducting qubit systems require control hardware with broad frequency coverage, low crosstalk, and tight synchronization, along with software that automates configuration and calibration.
method: The system combines broadband microwave hardware (1.6 GHz instantaneous span) with a pulse-level software stack for automated setup and experiment workflows. Validation is performed on a 64-qubit fixed-frequency transmon chip.
result: Full-chip frequency identification, multi-unit far-detuned cross-resonance calibration yields 98.34% two-qubit gate fidelity, and multilevel readout beyond the computational subspace is demonstrated.
conclusion: The open-source release of hardware architecture and software provides an inspectable foundation for scalable superconducting qubit control experiments.

title: Geometric Algebra Quantum Gate Decomposition
authors: Zeno Toffano Youssef Amraoui
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum gates are usually described through matrix and tensor-product formalisms that often obscure their geometric structure. In this work, we formulate the Pauli and Clifford groups within the complex Geometric Algebra (GA) framework. We show that the Pauli group is naturally identified with the group of blades up to a global phase, thereby providing a geometric interpretation of Pauli operators and their commutation relations in terms of oriented subspaces. title: Influence-solvability: A Systematic Theory Of $(1+1)d$ Solvability And Its Application To Brickwork Circuits
authors: Sun Woo P. Kim Friedrich H\"ubner
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: `Solvable' circuits, such as dual unitaries and its generalisations, have arisen as paradigmatic examples of tractable chaotic non-equilibrium dynamics, both in classical and quantum systems. However, while increasingly more complicated sufficient conditions have been proposed, a systematic theory classifying and understanding general features of solvable circuits is missing. We develop such a theory by introducing influence-solvable circuits, a class of [MATH] circuits whose influence matrix, which represents the `bath' generated by its own evolution, is given by a uniform MPS with finite bond-dimension [MATH]. This property allows for efficient computation of subsystem dynamics and essentially contains all known examples of solvable circuits. We derive a set of necessary and sufficient local conditions by using a version of the fundamental theorem of MPS for open boundary conditions. Next we apply our theory to brickwork circuits with [MATH] influence-solvability and perform a systematic classification of classical brickwork circuits with local dimension up to [MATH] and quantum brickwork circuits with [MATH]. Our search reveals new solvable circuits that are not captured by known solvability conditions.
tldr: Introduces influence-solvable circuits, a class of 1+1D circuits whose influence matrix is a uniform MPS, enabling efficient computation of subsystem dynamics and classification of solvable circuits.
motivation: Existing solvable circuits like dual unitaries lack a systematic theory; the authors aim to develop a unified framework to classify and understand all solvable circuits.
method: They define influence-solvability via the influence matrix being a uniform MPS with finite bond dimension, derive necessary and sufficient local conditions using the fundamental theorem of MPS, and perform a systematic classification of brickwork circuits.
result: The classification reveals new solvable circuits not captured by known conditions, and the framework unifies all known examples of solvable circuits.
conclusion: Influence-solvability provides a systematic theory for solvable circuits, enabling efficient computation and discovery of new solvable models.

The classification reveals new solvable circuits that were not captured by earlier solvability conditions, demonstrating the power of the influence-solvability framework.

title: Instabilities In A Non-KAM System Via Information Scrambling: A Note
authors: Naga Dileep Varikuti
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study operator growth in quantized non-KAM systems using out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs), focusing on the kicked harmonic oscillator as a representative example. Since the classical harmonic oscillator is degenerate, the dynamics fall outside the usual Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) framework, and resonances play a central role in shaping the phase space. We examine the system near resonances, where the ratio between the oscillator and driving frequencies takes integer values. Even though the classical Lyapunov exponent remains small at these points, and hence no conventional chaos, the phase space still undergoes strong structural changes. The OTOCs are particularly sensitive to these resonances, with a quadratic-in-time growth at resonance compared to linear growth away from it. Within a perturbative treatment, we derive closed-form expressions for the OTOCs and uncover a number-theoretic structure emerging in the behavior of OTOCs, governed by the Euler totient function of the frequency ratio. Overall, the results we present in this short note imply that resonant structures can play an important role in controlling information spreading.
tldr: This paper studies operator growth and information scrambling in a non-KAM quantum system (kicked harmonic oscillator) using OTOCs, revealing quadratic-in-time growth at resonances and a number-theoretic structure.
motivation: To understand how resonances affect information spreading in quantum systems that fall outside the KAM framework, where classical chaos is absent but phase space undergoes structural changes.
method: The authors compute out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) perturbatively for the quantized kicked harmonic oscillator near resonances, deriving closed-form expressions.
result: OTOCs exhibit quadratic-in-time growth at resonance compared to linear growth away from it, and the behavior is governed by the Euler totient function of the frequency ratio.
conclusion: Resonant structures can play an important role in controlling information spreading, even in the absence of conventional chaos.

The results suggest that resonant structures can significantly influence information spreading, even in the absence of classical chaos.

They treat the kicking strength as a small parameter and expand the time evolution operator to leading order. The OTOC is defined as the commutator squared of position operators at different times, averaged over a thermal state. By working in the interaction picture and using the harmonic oscillator eigenbasis, they derive analytic expressions for the OTOC as a function of time and the frequency ratio. The analysis focuses on resonant and near-resonant conditions, where the ratio of the oscillator frequency to the driving frequency is an integer. The perturbative treatment is valid for short times or weak kicking, and the authors check consistency with numerical simulations. The methodology is standard for OTOC calculations in weakly perturbed integrable systems.

The prefactor of the quadratic growth involves the Euler totient function φ(r), indicating a number-theoretic structure: the growth rate is proportional to φ(r) for prime r, and more generally to the sum of φ over divisors. title: Matrix Phase-space Representations For Quantum Symmetries
authors: Peter D. Drummond, Alexander S. Dellios, Margaret D. Reid
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a general phase-space representation that includes global quantum symmetries in the basis expansion. This method, called matrix phase-space, projects the basis onto a reduced Hilbert space, which can greatly reduce sampling errors of many-body quantum simulations and unifies several previous phase-space methods. The purpose of this paper is to provide detailed proofs of basic theorems and operator identities. We also treat several different types of symmetries. To illustrate the benefits of matrix phase-space methods, we give a detailed derivation of a recent application to the topical problem of verifying the outputs of Gaussian boson sampling (GBS) quantum computers with photon number resolving detectors. This has exponential complexity, and using parity symmetry reduces sampling errors by very large factors relative to earlier methods.
tldr: Introduces matrix phase-space representations incorporating global quantum symmetries to reduce sampling errors in many-body quantum simulations, with application to verifying Gaussian boson sampling.
motivation: Phase-space methods suffer from sampling errors that grow with system size; symmetries can reduce these errors but are not fully exploited in existing approaches.
method: Projects the basis onto a reduced Hilbert space using global symmetries, providing detailed proofs of operator identities and theorems for several symmetry types.
result: Demonstrates that parity symmetry reduces sampling errors by large factors in Gaussian boson sampling verification, which has exponential complexity.
conclusion: Matrix phase-space methods unify previous phase-space approaches and offer practical improvements for quantum simulations with symmetries.

title: Quantum Reservoir Computing For Short-Term Power Load Forecasting In Resource-Constrained Energy Systems
authors: Mansi Od, Param Pathak, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short-term load forecasting is essential for reliable energy management, but practical deployment on edge devices requires models that remain accurate under limited memory, finite measurement budgets, and hardware noise. This work proposes a hardware-efficient Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) framework for energy load forecasting, where a fixed quantum reservoir transforms temporal input windows into high-dimensional features and only a classical Elastic Net readout is trained. To reduce deployment cost, the trained readout is compressed using post-training fixed-point quantization at bit widths from 8 to 2 bits. The framework is evaluated on the Tetouan and Spain energy load datasets under exact statevector simulation, 512-shot finite sampling, and realistic hardware-noise models from IBM FakeTorino and IBM FakeMarrakesh. Results show that 6-bit readout precision preserves full-precision forecasting performance while reducing readout memory by 81.2%. Below this point, degradation becomes dataset dependent, with Tetouan showing stronger sensitivity and Spain degrading more gradually. Hardware-noise validation further shows that the trained readout transfers to noisy reservoir states without retraining. These findings support quantized QRC as a resource-aware forecasting approach for near-term quantum time-series applications.
tldr: This paper applies quantum reservoir computing to short-term power load forecasting, focusing on hardware efficiency and noise resilience.
motivation: Short-term load forecasting on edge devices requires models that are accurate under limited memory, finite measurement budgets, and hardware noise.
method: A fixed quantum reservoir transforms temporal inputs into high-dimensional features; only a classical Elastic Net readout is trained and then quantized to low bit widths.
result: 6-bit readout precision preserves full-precision performance while reducing memory by 81.2%; the readout transfers to noisy reservoir states without retraining.
conclusion: Quantized QRC is a resource-aware forecasting approach suitable for near-term quantum time-series applications on noisy hardware.

title: Experiment-compatible Measurement--feedback Quantum State Preparation With Reinforcement Learning
authors: Xiaotian Nie, Tao Zhang, Linghui Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ground-state preparation is a critical task in quantum simulation and quantum computing, as it enables the study of correlated phases and the generation of entangled resource states. While measurement--feedback control has emerged as a promising route to state preparation, existing schemes either rely on handcrafted, task-specific policies or are designed using full quantum-state information that is unavailable in real experiments and becomes impractical for large many-body systems. Here we develop an adaptive measurement--feedback protocol based on reinforcement learning under partial observability. The controller uses only the history of experimentally accessible measurement outcomes to choose both the measurement operator and the feedback action in real time. To make training compatible with experiments, we introduce a stochastic terminal reward built from one-shot measurements of randomly sampled Hamiltonian components, avoiding unphysical full-state reconstruction while remaining an unbiased estimator of the target energy. We demonstrate the method by preparing ground states of the Bose--Hubbard model and by generating GHZ states, establishing a scalable and hardware-compatible route to quantum state preparation.
tldr: A reinforcement learning-based measurement-feedback protocol for ground-state preparation using only experimentally accessible measurement outcomes.
motivation: Existing measurement-feedback state preparation schemes rely on handcrafted policies or full quantum-state information, which is impractical for experiments and large systems.
method: The controller uses a history of measurement outcomes to choose both measurement operator and feedback action, trained with a stochastic terminal reward from one-shot measurements of random Hamiltonian components.
result: Demonstrated on Bose-Hubbard model ground states and GHZ state generation, showing scalable and hardware-compatible state preparation.
conclusion: The protocol provides a practical, reinforcement learning-based approach to quantum state preparation that avoids full-state reconstruction and is compatible with experimental constraints.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents an adaptive measurement-feedback protocol for ground-state preparation in quantum systems, leveraging reinforcement learning under partial observability. The key innovation is that the controller uses only the history of measurement outcomes (not full quantum state information) to decide both which measurement to perform and what feedback action to apply. To train the reinforcement learning agent in a hardware-compatible way, the authors introduce a stochastic terminal reward based on one-shot measurements of randomly sampled Hamiltonian components, which provides an unbiased estimate of the energy without requiring full state tomography. The method is demonstrated on two tasks: preparing the ground state of the Bose-Hubbard model and generating GHZ states. The results show that the learned policy achieves high fidelity and low energy, comparable to or better than handcrafted strategies, while being scalable and experimentally feasible.
key_contributions: Development of a reinforcement learning framework for measurement-feedback control using only partial observability (measurement outcome history), eliminating the need for full quantum state information.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors formulate the state preparation as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where the agent's state is the history of measurement outcomes. The agent uses a recurrent neural network (RNN) to process this history and output actions: which measurement operator to apply and what feedback unitary to perform. Training is done via policy gradient methods (e.g., REINFORCE) with a reward function that is the negative of the estimated energy. The energy estimate is obtained by measuring a random Hamiltonian term at the end of the episode, which is unbiased due to the linearity of expectation. title: A Quantum Algorithm For Random Number Generation
authors: Aastha Kataria, Devansh Desai, Ashwini Dalvi, Sagar Korde, Abhijeet Pasi, Irfan N A Siddavatam, Sudhir Ranjan Jain
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a quantum algorithm for random number generation that achieves a provable quadratic speedup over classical Markov chain mixing, building on the Diaconis-Shahshahani Fourier analysis of the top-to-random card shuffle. The algorithm integrates three quantum primitives into a unified mixing circuit: the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT), which diagonalizes the Markov transition operator; controlled phase rotations, which encode the shuffle eigenvalue spectrum; and the Grover diffusion operator, which acts as a quantum analogue of the Aldous-Diaconis strong uniform stopping time by reflecting amplitudes about their mean at each iteration. For an n-qubit register, the mixing time is O() iterations. Extending to m qudits of local dimension d reduces this to O() iterations, where N = d^m, compared to the classical O(n \log n) bound. The qudit formulation further reduces QFT circuit depth from O(\log^2 N) to O(\log_d^2 N) gates per layer by encoding the same N-state space using m = \log_d N subsystems instead of \log_2 N qubits. We validate both variants on IBM superconducting hardware.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for random number generation using a quadratic speedup over classical Markov chain mixing via QFT, controlled phase rotations, and Grover diffusion.
motivation: To achieve faster random number generation by leveraging quantum speedups in mixing times for Markov chains.
method: Integrates QFT to diagonalize the Markov transition operator, controlled phase rotations to encode eigenvalues, and Grover diffusion as a quantum stopping time, applied to the top-to-random shuffle.
result: Mixing time of O(√N) for n-qubit register and O(√N) for m qudits, compared to classical O(n log n).
conclusion: The algorithm demonstrates a provable quadratic speedup and is validated on IBM hardware, but the contribution is more algorithmic than information-theoretic.

title: Error Probability Analysis Of Quantum Communication With Phase-squeezed M-psk
authors: Ioannis Krikidis Nikos A. Mitsiou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.13286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the symbol error probability (SEP) of phase-squeezed M-ary phase-shift keying (M-PSK). Since the relevant observable for M-PSK detection is the optical phase, we adopt the adaptive Mark-II receiver which is a physically realizable phase measurement. First, we develop a theoretical analysis based on the phase probability operator measure (POM) of the Mark-II scheme in the Fock basis. Then, we develop two SEP methods based on the statistics of the received PSK symbol and the error introduced by the Mark-II measurement. The first method derives the phase probability density induced by the squeezed state noise and incorporates the additional Mark-II phase uncertainty through an angular convolution. Since this convolution does not admit a simple closed form, we also introduce an effective tangential-variance model, which yields a closed form SEP expression in terms of the Owen's T-function. Numerical results show that phase squeezing substantially reduces the SEP of M-PSK compared to coherent state transmission, with greater gains for higher constellation orders. Notably, for the investigated scenario, squeezing can almost double the photon efficiency of M-PSK as the mean number of transmitted photons increases. Finally, the proposed approximations closely follow the Mark-II POM analysis, typically within an accuracy of 2-4 photons, and therefore provide accurate and computationally efficient tools for analyzing phase squeezed quantum M-PSK communication.
tldr: This paper analyzes the symbol error probability of phase-squeezed M-PSK in quantum communication using a Mark-II receiver, showing that squeezing improves photon efficiency.
motivation: To improve the error performance and photon efficiency of M-ary phase-shift keying in quantum communication by exploiting phase squeezing.
method: The authors develop a theoretical analysis based on the phase probability operator measure of the Mark-II receiver in the Fock basis, and propose two SEP methods: an angular convolution approach and an effective tangential-variance model yielding a closed-form expression.
result: Phase squeezing substantially reduces SEP compared to coherent states, with greater gains for higher constellation orders, and can almost double photon efficiency.
conclusion: The proposed approximations provide accurate and computationally efficient tools for analyzing phase-squeezed quantum M-PSK communication.

title: Handbook Of Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Philippe Faist Victor V. Albert
abstract: ArXiv:2606.11484v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Barcode scans, clear phone calls, reliable data storage, satellite communication, and large-scale quantum computation are all made possible by error correction. We present a handbook version of The Error Correction Zoo, a curated reference of methods for protecting classical or quantum information from errors during storage and transmission. The handbook includes descriptions of these error-correcting codes and a classification according to the symbols they use. It also catalogues relations among codes and related objects such as sphere packings, lattices, designs, groups, and classical and quantum phases of matter. The collection is intended both as a rigorous reference and as a practical aid for tracing the web of code relationships and uncovering new connections.

motivation: Error correction is essential for reliable communication and computation, and a comprehensive reference can aid researchers in navigating the vast landscape of codes.

conclusion: The handbook is a valuable resource for the error correction community, but as a reference work it does not present novel research results.

title: Sat, MaxSAT, And Smt For Qldpc Distance Computation: A Large-Scale Empirical Study
authors: Yu-Fang Chen, Seyed Mohammad Reza Jafari, Ching-Yi Lai
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12445v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exact distance computation for quantum LDPC (QLDPC) codes plays a central role in validating candidate fault-tolerant quantum-code constructions, yet the computational structure of this problem remains poorly understood. Despite substantial recent progress in QLDPC design, it remains unclear which algorithmic principles govern the practical scalability of exact distance computation and which classes of exact solvers are best suited to this task. To address these questions, we conduct a systematic study of SAT- and MaxSAT-based formulations for exact QLDPC distance computation across representative codes. We further compare these formulations against several established exact-distance approaches in order to better understand the algorithmic landscape of exact QLDPC distance computation. Our study challenges and refines several prevailing intuitions about exact QLDPC distance computation. First, despite the XOR-rich structure of QLDPC parity checks, practical scalability appears to be governed more by the handling of cardinality constraints and optimization bounds than by parity reasoning alone. Accordingly, XOR-aware reasoning does not provide a systematic advantage across our benchmark suite. Second, Brouwer-Zimmermann-style search, long regarded as the benchmark paradigm for exact distance computation in sparse classical codes, no longer maintains its traditional scalability advantage in the QLDPC setting. This finding challenges the expectation that techniques successful for sparse classical codes remain dominant for QLDPC codes. Third, substantial qualitative differences arise even among MaxSAT solvers themselves. Branch-and-bound MaxSAT significantly outperforms unsat-core-based MaxSAT on challenging benchmarks, demonstrating that solver architecture and optimization strategy play a decisive role in practical scalability.
tldr: A large-scale empirical study comparing SAT, MaxSAT, and SMT solvers for exact distance computation of QLDPC codes.
motivation: Exact distance computation is crucial for validating QLDPC codes, but the algorithmic landscape is poorly understood.
method: Systematic benchmarking of SAT- and MaxSAT-based formulations against established exact-distance approaches across representative QLDPC codes.
result: XOR-aware reasoning does not provide systematic advantage; Brouwer-Zimmermann search loses its traditional edge; branch-and-bound MaxSAT outperforms unsat-core-based MaxSAT.
conclusion: The study refines intuitions about QLDPC distance computation and highlights the importance of solver architecture and optimization strategy.

title: Thermodynamic Coefficients In Third-order Relativistic Fluid Dynamics
authors: Azwinndini Muronga Teboho Abram Moloi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We developed the third-order hydrodynamic equations using relativistic extended thermodynamics of gases with 14 independent fields. The resulting fluid equations are based on the relativity principle, the entropy principle, and the requirement of hyperbolic, and hence finite, propagation of disturbances, which is automatically incorporated. The expressions of entropy, four-current, shear-stress tensor, dynamic pressure, and heat flux are expanded up to third order (cubic). We explicitly present the newly calculated coefficients in the equilibrium properties of an ultra-relativistic gas regime and the non-degenerate relativistic gas. Contrary to the general cases, the non-degenerate regime eliminates fugacity from the coefficients, allowing for the easy normalization of these coefficients, and the ultra-relativistic regime provides us with the upper bounds of these coefficients. We found good agreement on some of the coefficients as compared to calculations from earlier models, specifically in kinetic theory, and other coefficients had slightly different values to those obtained in kinetic theory.
tldr: This paper derives third-order relativistic fluid dynamics equations using extended thermodynamics, focusing on thermodynamic coefficients for ultra-relativistic and non-degenerate gases.
motivation: To extend relativistic fluid dynamics beyond second order, ensuring hyperbolic equations and finite propagation speeds, and to compute higher-order transport coefficients.
method: Using relativistic extended thermodynamics with 14 independent fields, expanding entropy, currents, and dissipative fluxes up to third order, and applying the entropy principle and relativity principle.
result: Explicit expressions for third-order coefficients are obtained for ultra-relativistic and non-degenerate regimes; some coefficients agree with kinetic theory, others differ slightly.
conclusion: The third-order coefficients provide upper bounds and normalization, improving the accuracy of relativistic fluid dynamics for high-energy systems.

title: Unifying Spacetime Approaches To Quantum Mechanics
authors: N. L. Diaz, M. Cerezo, Paolo Braccia
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent efforts to formulate quantum mechanics in a way that treats space and time on a more equal footing have led to a large variety of spacetime-oriented approaches. In this work we present a detailed study of spacetime states, the objects that play the role of quantum states in the recently introduced framework of spacetime quantum mechanics, and show that the main proposals in the literature are different manifestations of the same underlying object. Path integrals, quantum states over time, pseudo-density matrices, the Page and Wootters mechanism, superdensity operators, and timelike-entanglement proposals all arise from spacetime states through particular evaluations, reduced information, linear maps, or quantum channels. This unification provides explicit mathematical representations of these formalisms, reveals relations among them, and clarifies the spacetime information each one captures. We also study the broader relevance of the spacetime-state point of view for Leggett-Garg inequalities, OTOCs, temporal tensor networks, fermionic systems, relativistic QFTs, quantum reference frames, and classical physics, together with additional insights and perspectives revealed by the common unifying framework.
tldr: This paper unifies various spacetime approaches to quantum mechanics by showing they arise from a common object called spacetime states.
motivation: To clarify the relationships among different spacetime-oriented formulations of quantum mechanics and to provide a unified mathematical framework.
method: The authors define spacetime states and demonstrate that path integrals, pseudo-density matrices, Page-Wootters mechanism, etc., are special cases obtained via evaluations, linear maps, or quantum channels.
result: All major spacetime approaches are manifestations of the same underlying spacetime state, with explicit mathematical representations and connections.
conclusion: The unified framework offers new insights into temporal correlations, quantum reference frames, and relativistic QFT, but does not directly advance core quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Roto-Reflection Geometry Of Pure Two-Qubit Entanglement
authors: Marcis Auzinsh Stanislav Filatov
abstract: ArXiv:2606.12637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pure two-qubit entanglement is usually characterized by scalar quantities such as concurrence. Here we show that it also has a natural geometric form. In the Pauli correlation tensor, maximally entangled states appear as improper orthogonal maps between two local Bloch spheres. These maps are roto-reflections. For partially entangled pure states, the same roto-reflection geometry is recovered after separating the contraction associated with concurrence. We call the corresponding geometric object the Entanglement Roto-Reflection Plane (ERRP). It organizes the maximally correlated directions of the two-qubit state and provides a covariant geometric complement to the scalar magnitude of entanglement.
tldr: The paper presents a geometric characterization of pure two-qubit entanglement using roto-reflections in the Pauli correlation tensor.
motivation: To provide a geometric complement to scalar entanglement measures like concurrence for pure two-qubit states.
method: Analyzes the Pauli correlation tensor of pure two-qubit states and shows that maximally entangled states correspond to improper orthogonal maps (roto-reflections) between local Bloch spheres.
result: Introduces the Entanglement Roto-Reflection Plane (ERRP) that organizes maximally correlated directions and provides a covariant geometric structure.
conclusion: The roto-reflection geometry offers a new perspective on two-qubit entanglement, but the contribution is primarily geometric and does not advance core topics like entanglement measures, nonlocality, or quantum cryptography.

The authors show that the Pauli correlation tensor of a pure two-qubit state can be decomposed into a product of a scalar (the concurrence) and an improper orthogonal matrix (a roto-reflection). For maximally entangled states, this tensor directly corresponds to a roto-reflection mapping between the local Bloch spheres. For partially entangled states, the same geometric structure is recovered after factoring out the concurrence. The authors define the Entanglement Roto-Reflection Plane (ERRP), which organizes the maximally correlated directions and provides a covariant geometric framework for understanding entanglement beyond its magnitude.

For pure states, the authors derive that T = c R, where c is the concurrence and R is an improper orthogonal matrix (det R = -1). This decomposition is obtained by analyzing the singular value decomposition of T and relating it to the Schmidt decomposition of the state. The authors then geometrically interpret R as a roto-reflection mapping between the Bloch spheres of the two qubits. The ERRP is defined as the plane orthogonal to the axis of the roto-reflection, which contains the directions of maximal correlation.

This implies that T is proportional to an orthogonal matrix. For maximally entangled states (c=1), T is exactly an improper orthogonal matrix. For partially entangled states, T/c is an improper orthogonal matrix. The authors show that the ERRP is spanned by the two singular vectors of T corresponding to the non-zero singular values (both equal to c). The plane is invariant under the roto-reflection, and its normal vector corresponds to the direction of the local Bloch vectors that are uncorrelated. The paper also discusses how the ERRP transforms under local unitary operations, demonstrating its covariance.
